figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: The H-PMP control architecture comprises a task-space admittance controller and a joint-space HapFIC. Task-Space: The system can implement either a traditional admittance behaviour or a HapFIC by altering how the admittance modifies $x^{\mathrm{des}}$ to yield $x^{\mathrm{adm}}$. This output is then passed to the Cartesian planner (Plan.) and a Task-Space FIC (FICTS), which consists of a 3D Cartesian controller and a quaternion controller. The resulting output wrench is transformed into the desired joint torques by pre-multiplying it by the Jacobian transpose ($J^{T}$). Joint-Space: The torque error $\tau_{\mathrm{des}}-\tau+g(q)$ is processed by the dead-band ($\mathrm{dz}^{h}$) described in Eq. (7) before being sent to the joint admittance block. The HapFIC algorithm (the joint-space HapFIC of Table I) within the joint admittance generates an offset $\delta$. This offset is added to the IK solution $q^{\mathrm{IK}}$—which is computed using $x^{\mathrm{adm}}$ as its input—to determine the admittance-modified joint angles $q^{\mathrm{adm}}$. These angles are subsequently sent as input to the Joint FICs (FICJS) to compute the FIC control torques $\tau^{J}$. Finally, the gravity vector $g(q)$ is added to $\tau^{J}$ to generate the final actuator control torques $\tau_{c}$.
figures.headline: Torque error passes through a dead-band and a joint-space FIC, with the task-space output mapped to joint torques by the Jacobian transpose.
citing_sentences: The H-PMP architecture, illustrated in Fig. 4, nests a task-space admittance or HapFIC controller (Admittance and HapFIC in task space, Table I) within a joint-space HapFIC (Table I).

The joint-space HapFIC then compares $\tau_{\mathrm{des}}$ with the net actuator torque (i.e., the measured actuator torque $\tau$ minus the gravity torque vector $g(q)$), which is compensated independently as depicted in Fig. 4.

abstract: Physical human–robot interaction requires controllers capable of maintaining intrinsically bounded interactions with the environment. The Fractal Impedance Controller (FIC) has been proven to guarantee these safety characteristics by design. This paper introduces the robotic implementation and experimental validation of its most advanced architecture: the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP), an evolution of the Passive Motion Paradigm designed to mimic human-like interaction. Furthermore, we present a unified framework for FIC deployment, supported by an open-source software suite featuring ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware integrations. Through three experiments conducted on a Kinova Gen3 arm (trajectory tracking, a wall press with sudden loss of contact, and learning-by-demonstration) we compare the H-PMP against earlier FIC architectures. The results demonstrate that the H-PMP achieves a seamless trade-off between admittance and impedance behaviours. This makes it ideal for deployment in unstructured environments, enabling the robot to transition between interaction modes with no computational overhead.

sections.body: Robots working in unstructured settings must handle expected and unexpected contact. Impedance control regulates position well, while admittance control regulates interaction force, and each carries the opposite limitation. The Fractal Impedance Controller (FIC) was introduced to overcome these limits. This paper packages FIC work into one open-source library. The library includes a robotic implementation of the H-PMP architecture, which the authors say can trade admittance and impedance without a rigid state machine. The library integrates MuJoCo, the Pinocchio library and ROS2. FIC Studio, a graphical interface, offers drag-and-drop tuning and Python live scripting. Fig. 1 shows the arm in two of the experiments.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Robots in unstructured settings need interaction control that trades admittance against impedance, and this paper packages FIC into one library.

sections.body: Redundant robots traditionally operated only in admittance or only in impedance mode, because the joint-to-task mapping is approximated with null-space projectors and has non-unique solutions. Optimisation-based methods such as Model Predictive Control enable trade-offs, but the authors note they are exposed to modelling errors, the sim-to-real gap, and numerical instability of the optimisation. FIC was introduced to exploit passivity. The authors say its state observer avoids the integration drift that affects non-passive systems. They distinguish purely passive controllers from passivated ones, which rely on energy tanks or virtual springs and remain susceptible to instability. H-PMP had only been partly ported to robotics before; this paper ports the complete architecture.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Redundant robots were restricted to one mode, and earlier trade-off methods risked instability, which FIC addresses through passivity.

sections.body: The suite has three components linked by ROS2 nodes: the graphical interface, the robot nodes that handle simulation and hardware, and the core FIC library. It runs natively on Linux with simulation and hardware, and on macOS with simulation only. A Docker version runs simulation on Windows, macOS and Linux. Each hardware vendor needs a driver that exchanges joint states and torques, plus a configuration file. Hardware has been tested on the Kinova Gen3 and the Franka FR3. Tuning profiles are stored as XML files, and saving a profile updates the running controller without a restart. The robot node runs the task-space layer on a 1 ms timer, and the joint inner loop runs at 1 kHz on hardware. The library can be deployed without the interface.
sections.heading: The FIC Suite
sections.headline: One FIC Studio graphical interface drives MuJoCo simulation and vendor hardware through the same library and profile files, tested so far on two arms.

sections.body: The effort function is linear near the desired state, with sigmoidal saturations on either side, and must be smooth with bounded derivatives. The FIC control law switches between a divergence phase, where the effort function applies, and a convergence phase, which gives a critically damped attractor. Orientation error is computed as a quaternion angle, and the torque is projected onto the end-effector frame. Admittance uses a user-set virtual inertia and viscosity rather than the robot's physical inertia, which the authors say makes it insensitive to kinematic singularities. In H-PMP, the task-space controller produces joint torques from the external wrench, and a joint-space controller compares them with measured torque minus gravity torque.
sections.heading: FIC Controllers
sections.headline: H-PMP nests a task-space admittance controller inside a joint-space FIC layer, with a shared FIC effort function underneath.

sections.body: All hardware experiments used a physical 7-DOF Kinova Gen3 arm. Experiment A tests trajectory tracking on a lemniscate. Experiment B tests a wall press followed by a sudden loss of contact. Experiment C compares H-PMP with Task-Space HapFIC for learning by demonstration. H-PMP is compared with three FIC architectures, each with its own tuning: a Cartesian impedance controller with a planner, a Task-Space HapFIC, and a Cartesian impedance controller with a joint-space HapFIC. Admittance controllers use an external wrench estimated from joint torques, because no force sensor is fitted to the Gen3. The experiments are open-source extensions of FIC Studio.
sections.heading: Experimental Validation
sections.headline: Three experiments on a Kinova Gen3 arm compare H-PMP with three other FIC architectures on tracking, contact loss and demonstration.

sections.body: The authors conclude that H-PMP offers a balanced compromise between impedance and admittance behaviour, letting the robot track trajectories while controlling interaction forces. They state that H-PMP is computationally efficient and could run entirely on a microcontroller with a maximum power consumption of approximately 400 mW, compared with the 15 W and 17 W drawn by the Arduino Ventuno Q board. The 400 mW figure is cited from a reference, not measured for H-PMP. The authors suggest online tuning could improve performance and make the architecture adaptive, and list adaptive tuning methods as future work. The FIC Suite is presented as enabling all available FIC architectures in MuJoCo simulation and on physical robots.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: H-PMP balances impedance and admittance, and the authors name adaptive online tuning as the next step.
